name: Nanochemistry
tagline: Design, synthesis, and application of nanoscale materials for medicine and energy.
seo_title: Nanochemistry — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Nanochemistry on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in nanoparticles, quantum dots, 2D materials and nanomedicine.

definition.lead: Nanochemistry makes and studies materials between about 1 and 100 nanometres in size, where size itself changes colour, reactivity and strength.
definition.body: A gold nanoparticle can look red, a semiconductor crystal can glow a colour set by its size, and a sheet of carbon one atom thick is remarkably strong. Nanochemists build these structures and put them to work in medicine, electronics, catalysis and energy.

facts.label: the nanoscale: a nanometre is a billionth of a metre
Richard Feynman's lecture 'There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom'

timeline.title: Colloidal gold
timeline.text: Michael Faraday prepares ruby-red gold colloids and studies how they scatter light.
timeline.why: The first scientific study of nanoparticles.

timeline.title: Plenty of room at the bottom
timeline.text: Richard Feynman imagines manipulating matter atom by atom.
timeline.why: Often cited as the vision behind nanotechnology.

timeline.title: Seeing atoms
timeline.text: Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer invent the scanning tunnelling microscope.

timeline.title: Fullerenes
timeline.text: Harold Kroto, Robert Curl and Richard Smalley discover C₆₀.
timeline.why: A new form of carbon; Nobel Prize in 1996.

timeline.title: Carbon nanotubes
timeline.why: Tiny tubes with exceptional strength and conductivity.

timeline.title: Quantum dots on demand
timeline.text: Moungi Bawendi's group makes high-quality quantum dots of controlled size.

timeline.title: Graphene
timeline.text: Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov isolate graphene with adhesive tape.
timeline.why: Launched the field of 2D materials; Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010.

timeline.title: DNA origami
timeline.text: Paul Rothemund folds DNA into designed shapes.

timeline.title: Nanoparticle vaccines
timeline.text: mRNA vaccines delivered by lipid nanoparticles are authorized.

timeline.title: Nobel Prize for quantum dots
timeline.text: Awarded to Moungi Bawendi, Louis Brus and Alexei Ekimov.

quiz.explain: A human hair is roughly 80,000–100,000 nm wide.

quiz.q: Why do quantum dots of different sizes emit different colours?
options: Confining electrons changes their energy levels: smaller dots emit bluer light
They are made of completely different elements
They have different coatings that tint the light
They are kept at different temperatures
quiz.explain: Same material, different size, different colour.

quiz.q: Why are nanoparticles such good catalysts?
options: They have a very high surface area per gram
They are heavier than bulk metals
They are magnetic and attract reactants
They are coloured and absorb light
quiz.explain: More atoms sit at the surface, where catalysis happens.

quiz.q: What colour are small gold nanoparticles in water?
quiz.explain: Their electrons oscillate with light and absorb green light.

options: A single layer of carbon atoms in a honeycomb lattice
A rolled-up tube of carbon atoms
A hollow sphere of 60 carbon atoms
A form of diamond only a few atoms thick
Like a cube with carbon corners

quiz.q: The scanning tunnelling microscope lets scientists…
quiz.explain: It measures a tiny current between a sharp tip and a surface.

quiz.q: What do lipid nanoparticles do in mRNA vaccines?
options: Protect the mRNA and help it enter cells
quiz.explain: Naked mRNA would be quickly destroyed.

options: Folding DNA into designed nanoscale shapes
quiz.explain: Short 'staple' strands fold a long strand into place.

quiz.q: Who first studied colloidal gold scientifically, in 1857?
quiz.explain: Some of his samples still exist.

quiz.q: The 2023 Nobel Prize in Chemistry rewarded…
options: The discovery and synthesis of quantum dots
quiz.explain: Graphene was the 2010 Physics prize; fullerenes the 1996 Chemistry prize.

quiz.q: As a particle gets smaller, its surface-to-volume ratio…
quiz.explain: Halving the size doubles the ratio.
